history.titleZh: PsiQuantum将其光子学技术转化为光开关，为AI数据中心GPU网络加速
history.descriptionZh:
PsiQuantum本周宣布，已将其低损耗硅光子技术转化为面向AI数据中心的光路交换机（OCS）。这一动向的背景是，随着AI集群规模扩大，GPU之间的数据通信正成为瓶颈；光互连相比铜缆具有更高带宽和更远传输距离，而全光交换机可避免传统数据中心交换机在每一跳都要进行光电转换所带来的功耗和延迟。OCS让光从光纤直接传到光纤，保持固定光路直到需要重新配置，其核心代价是光通过开关时的插入损耗。

传统数据中心交换机通常可容忍3 dB损耗，即约一半光信号损失。PsiQuantum展示的8×8 OCS原型在实验室测试中典型插入损耗仅1.2 dB，约损失四分之一的光，而且无需放大器。该开关基于硅芯片上蚀刻的光路，没有移动部件，区别于Google和Lumentum采用微机电系统（MEMS）微镜的方案。原型每输入均可到达任一输出，且“严格无阻塞”，新连接不会干扰已有连接；实测串扰为40 dB，约0.01%的光泄漏到其他端口，重构时间低于3毫秒，均超过公司为这些器件设定的初始目标。其损耗按光纤到光纤测量，包含光进出芯片，但不含连接器损耗。

不过，8×8端口规模仍明显小于竞争对手。Google的Palomar为136×136，典型插入损耗低于2 dB、最坏2 dB，采用毫秒级MEMS微镜；Lumentum R300为300×300，寿命初期典型损耗接近1.5 dB，也基于MEMS微镜；Salience Labs的OC-32M为32×32，端口间损耗低于2 dB，带内置放大，重构低于300微秒；iPronics ONE-32为32端口，未公布损耗，重构低于300微秒，带光放大器。PsiQuantum承认原型端口数更像演示平台，但已流片64×64版本，72×72正在开发，并称正在积极开发更大器件。公司还表示，未来产品损耗可能略高，但仍会保持很低。

低损耗来自其硅光子平台各环节的积累。PsiQuantum在2025年《Nature》论文中报告，硅氮化物波导损耗低至每米0.5 dB，约每米损失11%的光；分束器损耗0.5毫dB，交叉结构1.2毫dB，均仅为百分之几甚至更低；芯片到光纤耦合的最佳公布实验室结果约为60毫dB，约损失1.4%的光，但当时未连接完整光纤阵列。公司提醒，这些是最佳情况而非最坏情况，端口增加到64个后光会经过更多组件，损耗会累加。

在系统兼容性方面，OCS可接受的损耗取决于链路两端的光模块。Coherent称使用OCS可能增加最多3 dB额外插入损耗，但其收发器可承受；Lumentum则表示3 dB足以配合现成的FR4、DR4和DR8光模块，这些模块用于连接GPU服务器和交换机，距离为500米至2公里。PsiQuantum的8×8器件工作在O波段，正是这些模块使用的波长范围。公司称，其开关要具备可用性，插入损耗需低于2至3 dB；8×8原型面向常规数据中心流量设计，已低于Nvidia提案请求中3 dB的损耗目标。

在应用上，目前OCS的速度重要性低于插入损耗。Google部署量最大，达“数万”台，主要用于调整TPU pod规模或绕过故障芯片，毫秒级MEMS开关即可胜任。PsiQuantum低于3毫秒的重构时间属于同一量级，但Salience和iPronics宣称低于300微秒，iPronics尤其强调可在工作负载运行期间重新配置网络，以隐藏切换时间。PsiQuantum表示速度仍有很大提升空间，并已有钛酸钡（BTO）材料路径：BTO在施加电压时改变光的偏折方式，公司称其效应强于更常见的铌酸锂，可使切换元件更短、损耗更低，速度比当前演示快约百万倍。BTO并非演示产品或初始产品所必需，当前产品使用热切换硅氮化物平台，但它是未来更高速、更先进产品的额外路径。

PsiQuantum认为，现在为常规应用制造数千台此类开关，可降低其量子计算所用部件的封装、组装和供应链风险，并称AI与量子计算是“互补技术”。公司7月聘请Rob Soderbery担任执行副总裁，以推进硅光子平台在AI网络等下一代计算基础设施中的应用；其CHIPS项目奖励也于9月最终确定，涵盖“高性能光开关”等组件。联合创始人Pete Shadbolt称赞Google的MEMS方案，但更希望在同一单片芯片上实现同等质量、无需移动部件的开关。Nvidia通过风险投资部门NVentures持有PsiQuantum股份，并在“GPU-QPU集成”和硅光子方面与其合作；Nvidia还在9月参与了竞争对手iPronics的1.25亿美元融资，用于开发第二代光开关。

市场层面，Google内部已用OCS重构AI集群，研究机构Cignal AI预计到本十年末多数部署仍将集中在这一场景；Google之外，OCS仍处于“概念验证和早期试验”阶段。不过该机构今年早些时候上调了市场预测，2026年约上调三倍，2029年上调超过40%。PsiQuantum在GPU网络中存在机会，这也与Nvidia的兴趣相关，但预计采用规模在届时之前仍有限。公司称样品和测试套件已送往多家计算公司，包括GPU厂商和超大规模云厂商。PsiQuantum应在“未来数月”宣布商业产品及更大器件进展；竞争对手Salience已在今年欧洲光通信会议上展示64端口，路线图包括128和256端口。规模扩展始终是挑战，但如果PsiQuantum尚未经独立验证的数据能在64端口、无放大器条件下保持，更大规模的单片OCS将有望到来。

history.title: A primer on key AI LLM concepts — KV cache, weights, quantization, and how inference actually works
history.description: How do AI models work? This primer explains crucial concepts to understand how LLMs work, with definitions and explanations for all of AI's new nomenclature.
history.content: Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter As hardware for running local AI models continues to move to the forefront, such as Nvidia's RTX Spark, a new set of acronyms, definitions, and terminology is popping up. Given the pace of releases, we've put together a list of AI's new nomenclature to familiarize you with new concepts and pieces of terminology that you'll likely see in Tom's Hardware Premium articles.This primer should get you started on the world of AI and be handy the next time news on the topic comes around, and possibly when you're downloading some models to try out and tweak for yourself. For the context of this article, we're going to stick with notions related to text LLMs, or in common parlance, chat, programming, and most agentic bots.ModelThis is probably the easiest one: a model is the LLM itself (a Large Language Model), computed from training sets of mostly text data on the scale of terabytes to petabytes. That training information comes from the internet, books, video and audio transcripts, and other sources.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: The model is roughly analogous to a set of highly advanced layers of statistical analysis of relationships between tokens — words or parts of words, computer code, punctuation, and other symbols. The tokens themselves aren't part of the model, but they are packaged along with it. An AI model generates tokens in its outputs.WeightsThose computing layers within an AI model would be useless without corresponding weights, which represent how strong the connection is between sections of tokens, sort of like how a pathway between neurons is more traveled than others. When the model runs, these values end up establishing how tokens end up relating to each other. You may like Benchmarking Qwen 3.8 27B on RTX 5090 and beyond Our first step at defining a CPU benchmark for agentic AI OpenAI Jalapeño design interview transcript Example: the weights of the connections between "na" and each next part for "naval", "nachos", or "naruto" will all be different, and the higher the weight, the more often that word appears in training data. Importantly, weights cannot change without re-training the model, or parts of it.When you see LLM specs online, you'll see something like "4B", "8B+", "20B", and so on and so forth. That shows how many parameters, or weights, the model uses, and it's generally measured in billions for consumer-grade models, and trillions for frontier models like GPT, Claude, and Kimi.Note that a model having more weights than another doesn't automatically mean it's smarter. Just like with CPU clock speeds, it's not just about getting a higher number — bigger is usually better, yes, but you want those weights to be meaningful for the output.You may also have heard about "open-weight" models versus "closed" models. Those refer to models like Llama, DeepSeek, and Kimi, which are effectively free-to-use, since the entities behind them freely publish the weights online. You can tweak the weights to your heart's content, if you wish, and come up with your own spin on things, as long as you have the hardware to run it. Note that downloading a free model doesn't reveal anything about how it was trained or how the weights were calculated — think downloading a free customizable application, not open-source software.Data types and quantizationFP16, INT8, FP4, all sound like acronyms in some military handbook, but they're simple to interpret. All programs use numbers of varying width and precision, depending on their purpose: a simple money counter in your favorite game might be fine with a 32-bit integer that can represent 0 to 2^32 (INT32), while a value held in memory for a highly precise scientific measurement may need floating-point 64-bit arithmetic (FP64). What to read next Frontier AI faces pricing reckoning as token volume explodes 25-fold Deepseek's latest AI model is smarter than ever, but its low running costs come at a price 'AI Torture Chamber' triggers massive backlash for putting chatbots in simulated pain As memory is an exceedingly finite resource, good developers try to use the smallest units they can get away with, a notion that's particularly important in the VRAM-limited world of GPUs. Predictably, these chips became particularly adept at handling lower-precision values as a tradeoff between processing speed and numerical accuracy. A particular datatype isn't better or worse, as that assessment will depend on what it's used for.When training an AI model, the labs will want to use as high a precision as they can for the weights, but keeping that in the final version would make for a prohibitively large and slow LLM. That's where the concept of quantization comes in, which is a fancy word for "clever rounding." As one of the steps after training, several passes are made to transform highly precise weights. Each AI lab has its own secret sauce about how to do this, as it's a critical step.Frontier models predominantly use relatively high precision for their weights (BF16), in order to maintain response quality, nuance, and reasoning ability (an analogy would be deciding how accurate you want a GPS location to be — miles or inches). Open-weight models often have several versions with different quantization levels depending on what your hardware can bear — for example, Llama 3.3 70B can be run in full BF16 or quantized INT4 flavors.The lower the precision, the more likely it can be run on consumer hardware. AI models listed on Hugging Face may have several quantization levels to fit certain levels of hardware, trading response accuracy for size. Consumer-grade models use smaller data types so they can fit on your Mac Studio, RTX Spark, or graphics card.Context window"Context window" is another term you've heard a lot and probably seen firsthand, likely in Claude Code's UI as a broad indicator of how long your session can go before the bot starts acting a little dumb. It's measured in tokens, with one million being a common number for frontier models, and it's almost directly analogous to RAM in a computer.The context window is the LLM's thinking space, and it needs to contain everything associated with your session, not just the current question. Along with all your questions and its replies, it contains system-level prompts, all files you uploaded, the content of links it looked up, plus any associated data.Crucially, while for you all these things are distinct concepts, for the LLM, they get reduced to tokens in one large pile: the context window. This is also why separating "data" from "code" is technically impossible — the best that modern models do is an approximation of that distinction.LLMs don't think — when answering a new question, they re-run a statistics program over all the tokens and predict the next handful, so having a larger context window is beneficial (at the cost of VRAM), hence the one-million figure that's currently popular. But even statistical algorithms have their limits.Even if you increase the window to, say, three million tokens, you may find that your LLM's prediction starts breaking down even though it hasn't run out. This is amusingly called the "lost in the middle" effect, where the bot will pay attention to the start and end of the conversation but will forget things down the middle. Thus, each model is finely tuned to the size of its context window.KV CacheIf you've looked into using LLMs locally, or by way of running a remote GPU, you may have heard about the "KV cache" time and again, and that you need to reserve VRAM for it, or store it on a fast SSD if you absolutely must. This is a set of data that's created when the model runs, but that's actually reusable between queries in the same session.The data that's saved and reused can be described as "the relations between tokens for this session." For example, the ever-popular sentence "you're right to push back" can be tokenized as "you-'re-ri-ght-to-pu-sh-back". The dashes between each token represent a vector (or array), called KV for key-value, that is used for determining which token gets picked next.Since the text generation is linear, the math for calculating each new token needs every KV preceding it. Thus, if you're asking repeated questions in the same session, you'll want the KVs reused to avoid the expense of recalculating them over and over again not just with each round of conversation, but with each additional token.Remember, an LLM doesn't simply answer the question you just posted — it always analyzes the entire conversation from the top to eventually generate tokens for your response. In a long conversation with 300,000 tokens, not having the cache would mean recalculating the KVs for all of them, a slow operation that gets disproportionately slower still as the interactions grow. This excellent blog post has a more detailed example.Remember quantization? That's also applied here — modern models reduce the precision of the KV cache's content compared to their initial values, trading a minor accuracy loss for all new tokens in the session, in exchange for keeping VRAM usage down. In fact, with large context windows and conversations, the KV cache may well eat more space than the model and weights themselves.Mixture-of-Experts (MoE)Previously, AI firms touted how many more parameters their newest model had. Now, the race seems to have shifted to who can include more experts in any given model. That description may conjure a mental image of many tiny scientists living inside a knowledge laboratory, each handling a specific topic, but that's not quite how it works.Mixture-of-experts, or MoE, is essentially a set of sub-models within the main model. When training starts, all sub-models get the same dataset, but the choice of weights is randomized ever so slightly for each one. Each sub-model will value tokens a bit differently from the rest, and due to how the training process reinforces patterns (called the "rich-get-richer" effect), related tokens will tend to converge together, so you end up with "experts" on sets of tokens.A common misconception is to think that these experts are related to topics (like programming), but they're only establishing relations between tokens, meaning they'll be more accurate for certain words and text patterns, but devoid of any concept of what they're about. The fact that an expert might offer pretty good responses in regard to landscape painting is a happy accident, not a feature.You may be thinking that this makes the models larger, and that maybe just the one generalist expert may prove a wiser choice. That's correct, but the trick is that the models only activate certain experts, meaning that only a portion of the model is actually running, thus at higher speed than a generic LLM.This model selection happens on a per-token basis, too, as a router re-selects experts for each incoming token. For visualizing this, think of brain scan patterns where different areas light up depending on words heard. In practical terms, it means the model can answer more accurately in certain sections, while answering the question faster — albeit at the cost of higher VRAM usage.Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)RAG is a concept that's pretty easy to describe, and yet one of the most powerful ones when used with any given model. In short, it can be described as: your chat application runs a few Google searches, feeds them to the model, and voila, there's now much more and fresher information to answer your question. This additional information can come in most any form: company documents, reports, emails, or spreadsheets — anything that you might supply to the model yourself, directly tokenized into its context window.While broadly speaking most contemporary LLM chat applications run searches, activating RAG, usually triggered by selecting a "web search" switch or sometimes enabling "thinking" or "high effort" mode, will explicitly instruct the application to find as much data as it believes necessary to answer a query. Given that pure context is often key to answering many questions, and do so in an informational manner, RAG is among the most powerful tools available.Fun fact: the search queries the application will search for are usually generated by a smaller, separate model that will, for example, say what web searches are bound to give the best results, or what to look for in a linked Office 365 account.The main drawback is that it can be extremely computing-intensive, as the text for your questions and responses may consume, say, 10,000 tokens, yet the information in the retrieved webpages can take hundreds of thousands of tokens all on their own. For example, the Perplexity service was built with an emphasis on RAG usage, and judging from personal experience and user reports, it's usually much more competent and context-aware when answering questions, even though it's underpinned by the same models as everyone else.Inference, Prefill and DecodeInference is the act of using a trained model to generate outputs or tokens. It happens every time you send a prompt, and it's where all of the elements that we've discussed above come into play. Inference can be split into two primary parts: Prefill and Decode.Prefill is the first phase of inference. Essentially, all of the input history (or your prompt) is tokenized and then processed by an AI model. This can include documents, code, and more. These inputs also dictate what gets put into your KV cache. Prefill is processed all at once in parallel, which often means that prefill times are often faster than overall outputs.Prefill is a large part of the overall workload when measuring how long it takes for a specific chip or piece of hardware can take to output its first token, also known as "time to first token" (TTFT), a common AI benchmark, usually reported alongside prefill tokens per second. Longer prompts take longer to prefill, and context, KV cache, and everything else we've discussed are taken into account.Decode is the second phase of inference. After a prefill has processed your input and has built the KV cache, the AI model then generates its response one token at a time, which must be done sequentially in order to determine the ones that come after, which means that the step cannot be performed in parallel, unlike prefill. Decode is usually also dictated by context, and reads from a model's KV cache during this step. Decode is usually limited by memory bandwidth, instead of raw compute, as streaming single tokens from weights and reading the KV cache is a bandwidth-intensive task, meaning memory speeds matter more. You'll usually see Decode speeds referred to as tokens-per-second (TPS).Speculative Decode is a technique that makes those single tokens in the decode step stream faster, without changing the overall output. A drafting mechanism guesses several upcoming tokens, and then the model attempts to verify them in a parallel pass (almost like an additional prefill step). The model then verifies the pass itself; if the guesses are good, then the model's outputs are indeed correct, you get tokens for less of a computational cost during a given decode pass, and when they're bad, they are rejected by the main model during verification, since the main model's output is always what's kept.Multi-token prediction (MTP) attempts to predict the next set of tokens at once, rather than only serving the next token. This is often built into AI models when they are trained with multiple steps. This can serve as the built-in drafting mechanism required for speculative decode.This is a non-exhaustive list of concepts critical to understanding how AI models and LLMs work, but it is by no means complete. We will continue to update and refine this article as we add more.
history.author: Bruno Ferreira
history.titleZh: AI LLM 关键概念入门——KV 缓存、权重、量化，以及推理究竟如何运作
history.descriptionZh:
随着在本地运行AI模型的硬件不断走向前台，例如Nvidia的RTX Spark，一系列新的缩写、定义和术语正在涌现。鉴于发布节奏之快，我们整理了一份AI新术语清单，帮助读者熟悉在Tom's Hardware Premium文章中可能遇到的新概念和术语。这份入门指南旨在帮助读者进入AI世界，并在下次相关新闻出现时派上用场，或许还能在你下载一些模型自行尝试和调整时提供帮助。本文聚焦于文本大语言模型（LLM）相关概念，即通常所说的聊天、编程以及大多数智能体机器人。

模型（Model）：模型就是LLM本身（大语言模型），由主要来自文本数据的训练集计算而来，数据规模从数TB到数PB不等。训练信息来自互联网、书籍、视频和音频转录以及其他来源。模型大致相当于对令牌（单词或单词的一部分、计算机代码、标点符号和其他符号）之间关系进行高度先进的统计分析的多层结构。令牌本身不属于模型，但会与模型一起打包。AI模型在输出中生成令牌。

权重（Weights）：AI模型内部的计算层若无相应的权重便毫无用处，权重表示令牌各部分之间连接的强度，类似于神经元之间的通路有的比其他通路更常被使用。当模型运行时，这些值决定了令牌之间最终如何关联。例如，“na”与“naval”“nachos”或“naruto”各自后续部分之间的连接权重都会不同，权重越高，该词在训练数据中出现的频率越高。重要的是，权重在不重新训练模型或其部分的情况下无法改变。在网上查看LLM规格时，会看到“4B”“8B+”“20B”等字样，这表示模型使用的参数或权重数量，消费级模型通常以十亿计，而GPT、Claude和Kimi等前沿模型则以万亿计。需要注意的是，模型权重更多并不自动意味着更聪明。就像CPU时钟频率一样，数字更高通常更好，但关键在于这些权重对输出是否有意义。读者可能还听说过“开放权重”模型与“封闭”模型的区别。前者如Llama、DeepSeek和Kimi，实际上可免费使用，因为其背后的实体在网上公开发布权重。只要有硬件运行，就可以随意调整权重，打造自己的版本。注意，下载免费模型并不会揭示其训练方式或权重计算方法——可以将其理解为下载一个免费的可定制应用，而非开源软件。

数据类型与量化：FP16、INT8、FP4听起来像某本军事手册里的缩写，但其实很容易理解。所有程序都根据用途使用不同宽度和精度的数字：游戏中的简单计钱器用32位整数（INT32，可表示0到2^32）就够了，而高精度科学测量值可能需要浮点64位运算（FP64）。由于内存是极其有限的资源，优秀的开发者会尽量使用最小的单位，这在GPU显存受限的环境中尤为重要。这些芯片因此特别擅长处理低精度值，作为处理速度与数值精度之间的权衡。特定数据类型本身没有好坏之分，评估取决于用途。训练AI模型时，实验室希望权重使用尽可能高的精度，但保留在最终版本中会使LLM过大过慢。这就是量化概念的用武之地，简单说就是“巧妙的舍入”。作为训练后的步骤之一，会进行多轮处理来转换高精度权重。每个AI实验室都有自己的秘方，因为这是关键步骤。前沿模型主要使用相对高精度的权重（BF16），以保持响应质量、细微差别和推理能力（类比：决定GPS定位精度是英里还是英寸）。开放权重模型通常有多个不同量化级别的版本，取决于硬件承受能力——例如Llama 3.3 70B可以全BF16运行，也可以INT4量化版本运行。精度越低，越可能在消费级硬件上运行。Hugging Face上列出的AI模型可能有多个量化级别以适应不同硬件水平，以响应准确性换取体积。消费级模型使用较小的数据类型，以便能装进Mac Studio、RTX Spark或显卡中。

上下文窗口（Context window）：这是另一个常听到的术语，可能已在Claude Code界面中亲眼见过，大致指示会话能持续多久而不至于让机器人开始变笨。它以令牌计量，前沿模型常见的一百万是一个常见数字，几乎可以直接类比为计算机中的RAM。上下文窗口是LLM的思考空间，需要包含与会话相关的所有内容，不仅是当前问题。除了所有问题和回复外，它还包含系统级提示、上传的所有文件、查阅链接的内容以及任何相关数据。关键在于，虽然对用户来说这些都是不同的概念，但对LLM而言，它们都被简化为一个大队列中的令牌：上下文窗口。这也是为什么从技术上不可能将“数据”与“代码”分开——现代模型做的最多只是近似区分。LLM并不思考——回答新问题时，它们对所有令牌重新运行统计程序并预测接下来的几个令牌，因此更大的上下文窗口是有益的（代价是显存），这就是当前流行的一百万数字的由来。但即使是统计算法也有极限。即使将窗口增加到三百万令牌，可能会发现LLM的预测在尚未用尽时就开始崩溃。这被戏称为“中间迷失”效应，即机器人会关注对话的开头和结尾，但会忘记中间的内容。因此，每个模型都针对其上下文窗口大小进行了精细调优。

KV缓存（KV Cache）：如果研究过本地使用LLM或通过远程GPU运行，可能反复听到“KV缓存”，需要为其预留显存，或者万不得已时存储在快速SSD上。这是模型运行时创建的一组数据，但实际上可在同一会话的查询之间重复使用。保存和复用的数据可以描述为“本会话中令牌之间的关系”。例如，那句流行的“you're right to push back”可以被令牌化为“you-'re-ri-ght-to-pu-sh-back”。每个令牌之间的破折号代表一个向量（或数组），称为KV（键值），用于确定下一个选择哪个令牌。由于文本生成是线性的，计算每个新令牌的数学需要前面所有的KV。因此，如果在同一会话中反复提问，就会希望复用KV，以避免不仅在每轮对话中、而且在每个额外令牌上反复重新计算的开销。记住，LLM不是简单地回答刚发布的问题——它总是分析整个对话从头开始，最终生成回复的令牌。在30万令牌的长对话中，没有缓存意味着要重新计算所有令牌的KV，这是一个缓慢的操作，而且随着交互增长会变得不成比例地更慢。量化也应用在这里——现代模型降低了KV缓存内容相对于初始值的精度，以会话中所有新令牌的轻微准确性损失换取显存占用的降低。事实上，在大上下文窗口和长对话中，KV缓存占用的空间可能比模型和权重本身还多。

混合专家（Mixture-of-Experts, MoE）：以前，AI公司吹嘘其最新模型有多少参数。现在，竞赛似乎转向了谁能在给定模型中包含更多专家。这个描述可能让人联想到知识实验室里有许多小科学家各自处理特定主题，但事实并非如此。MoE本质上是主模型内的一组子模型。训练开始时，所有子模型获得相同的数据集，但每个子模型的权重选择会略微随机化。每个子模型对令牌的估值会略有不同，由于训练过程强化模式的方式（称为“富者愈富”效应），相关令牌倾向于汇聚在一起，最终形成针对令牌集合的“专家”。一个常见的误解是认为这些专家与主题（如编程）相关，但它们只是建立令牌之间的关系，这意味着它们对某些词和文本模式更准确，但完全没有关于内容主题的概念。某个专家可能在风景画方面给出相当好的回答，这是意外之喜，而非设计特性。读者可能认为这会使模型更大，或许一个通用专家可能是更明智的选择。没错，但诀窍在于模型只激活某些专家，意味着只有部分模型实际运行，因此速度比通用LLM更快。这种模型选择也是基于每个令牌进行的，路由器会为每个传入令牌重新选择专家。可视化理解：想象大脑扫描模式，不同区域根据听到的词而亮起。实际而言，这意味着模型在某些部分能更准确地回答，同时回答更快——代价是更高的显存占用。

检索增强生成（Retrieval-Augmented Generation, RAG）：RAG概念很容易描述，但与任何给定模型配合使用时却是最强大的概念之一。简而言之：聊天应用运行几次谷歌搜索，将结果喂给模型，瞧，现在有更多更新的信息来回答问题了。这些额外信息可以采取多种形式：公司文档、报告、邮件或电子表格——任何可以自己提供给模型、直接令牌化到上下文窗口中的内容。虽然广义上讲大多数当代LLM聊天应用都会运行搜索，但激活RAG（通常通过选择“网络搜索”开关或有时启用“思考”或“高努力”模式触发）会明确指示应用找到它认为回答问题所需的尽可能多的数据。鉴于纯上下文通常是回答许多问题的关键，并且以信息丰富的方式做到这一点，RAG是可用最强大的工具之一。有趣的是，应用要搜索的查询通常由一个小型的独立模型生成，例如说明哪些网络搜索最可能给出最佳结果，或在关联的Office 365账户中查找什么。主要缺点是计算强度可能极高，因为问题和回复的文本可能消耗比如1万令牌，而检索网页中的信息可能单独占用数十万令牌。例如，Perplexity服务在构建时就强调RAG使用，从个人经验和用户报告来看，它在回答问题时通常更有能力、更具上下文意识，尽管其底层模型与其他家相同。

推理、预填充与解码（Inference, Prefill and Decode）：推理是使用训练好的模型生成输出或令牌的行为。每次发送提示时都会发生，也是上述所有元素发挥作用的地方。推理可分为两个主要部分：预填充和解码。预填充是推理的第一阶段。基本上，所有输入历史（或提示）被令牌化，然后由AI模型处理。这可以包括文档、代码等。这些输入也决定了KV缓存中放入什么。预填充是并行一次性处理的，这通常意味着预填充时间往往快于整体输出。在衡量特定芯片或硬件输出第一个令牌所需时间（即“首令牌时间”，TTFT，常见AI基准，通常与预填充令牌每秒一起报告）时，预填充是总工作量的重要部分。提示越长，预填充时间越长，上下文、KV缓存以及讨论过的所有其他内容都会被考虑在内。解码是推理的第二阶段。预填充处理完输入并构建KV缓存后，AI模型然后逐个令牌生成回复，必须顺序进行以确定后续令牌，这意味着该步骤不能像预填充那样并行执行。解码通常也由上下文决定，并在此步骤中读取模型的KV缓存。解码通常受内存带宽而非原始计算能力限制，因为从权重流式传输单个令牌和读取KV缓存是带宽密集型任务，意味着内存速度更重要。解码速度通常以每秒令牌数（TPS）表示。推测解码（Speculative Decode）是一种使解码步骤中的单个令牌流更快而不改变整体输出的技术。起草机制猜测几个即将出现的令牌，然后模型尝试在并行通道中验证它们（几乎像额外的预填充步骤）。模型然后验证该通道本身；如果猜测良好，模型的输出确实正确，则在给定解码通道中以更少的计算成本获得令牌；当猜测不佳时，主模型在验证期间拒绝它们，因为主模型的输出始终是保留的。多令牌预测（Multi-token prediction, MTP）尝试一次预测下一组令牌，而不是仅提供下一个令牌。这通常在AI模型训练时以多个步骤内置。这可以作为推测解码所需的内置起草机制。

这是一份理解AI模型和LLM工作原理的关键概念的非详尽清单，但绝非完整。随着我们添加更多内容，我们将继续更新和完善本文。

history.title: Benchmarking Nvidia’s Vera CPU for the data center — standalone Vera tested against Granite Rapids-AP and EPYC Turin
history.description: Nvidia gave us access to its Vera data center CPU for testing against Intel's Granite Rapids-AP and AMD's EPYC Turin.
history.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 4 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Nvidia’s Vera CPU is an important next step in the company’s years-long spearheading of AI infrastructure buildout. It’s arriving just as the shift to agentic AI workflows has created unprecedented demand for data center CPUs, and it’s designed specifically for this moment, at least according to Nvidia’s marketing bullet points. Although the idea that anyone developed a CPU for a shift in demand that arose just six months ago is reaching, as our benchmarks below show, Nvidia’s claims about Vera aren’t full of hot air.Based on the workloads we have now — there aren’t standardized end-to-end agentic benchmarks focused on the CPU right now — Vera has strong indicators about its usefulness in agentic workflows. It offers chart-topping performance in Python, for instance, which makes up much of the backbone of the AI software ecosystem.It also shows commanding memory bandwidth, both at the socket level and system level, with the high-speed C2C interconnect between Vera chips. In contentious agentic environments where agents may be querying large databases, that bandwidth is critical.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: Specialization is one thing, but Vera is arriving in a hotly contested server market with custom Arm chips penetrating the data center and the old guard of x86 chips from AMD and Intel, which not only have a foundation in the data center, but also an extensive list of clients that work with their systems. Regardless of how Vera performs, that’s no small undertaking.What’s surprising about Vera isn’t that it performs well in these agentic-adjacent workloads, but that it offers competent performance in general-purpose server workloads as well, often managing to match or beat the comparable AMD Turin and Intel Granite Rapids-AP chips. The scales are more balanced when looking at frontend workloads, with the core density available on x86 CPUs often the winner, but Vera trades that density for strong performance in backend, data-rich operations. You may like Standalone Nvidia Vera CPUs land in Oracle Cloud's multi-gigawatt deployment Hot Chips 2026: Nvidia breaks down 88-core Vera CPU AMD targets Nvidia with first official benchmarks for EPYC 'Venice' CPUs Swipe to scroll horizontally Nvidia Vera specifications Cores / Threads 88 / 176 L2 cache 2 MB per core L3 cache 164 MB per CPU Memory Up to 1.5 TB SOCAMM2 LPPDDR5X Memory speed Up to 9600 MT/s Memory bandwidth Up to 1.2 TB/s (aggregate), 14 GB/s (per core) PCIe 88 PCIe 6.4 lanes (CPU only), 96 PCIe 6.4 lanes (Vera Rubin), bifurcation down to x2, CXL 3.1 Configurable TDP 250W - 450W It’s an impressive showing for Nvidia's first custom core, called Olympus, and a stark improvement in nearly all aspects over Grace, which used an off-the-shelf Arm core design. The 88-core CPU is built on the Armv9.2-A architecture, including two threads per core through Nvidia’s “spatial multithreading.”The chip is characterized by a 10-wide decode, similar to Arm’s AGI, as well as Nvidia’s second-gen Scalable Coherency Fabric (SCF). You can read more about the SCF and the Olympus core in our Vera deep dive, but SCF is critical to Vera’s performance. It’s a mesh that distributes L3 across the die, offering up to 3.4 TB/s of bandwidth across the die.Stay On the Cutting Edge: Get the Tom's Hardware NewsletterGet Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsorsVera has high memory bandwidth as well, leveraging replaceable SOCAMM2 LPDDR5X at 9600 MT/s, offering up to 1.2 TB/s of total memory bandwidth or around 14 GB/s per core, more than double that of AMD’s dense Turin designs.We’ve heard a lot about the speeds and feeds of Vera, however. It’s time to understand its role in the modern AI data center, as well as see how it performs in our benchmarks against the x86 competition before AMD’s Venice and Intel’s Diamond Rapids start rolling out. Swipe to scroll horizontally Test platforms Test Platform Memory Tested Processors 2P Nvidia MGX Vera reference platform 16 x 96 GB (1.5 TB) Samsung LPDDR5-9600 ECC SOCAMM2 Nvidia Vera 2P Supermicro SYS-222HA 24 x 64GB (1.5 TB) Micron DDR5-8800 ECC MRDIMM Intel Xeon 6980P 2P AMD Volcano reference platform 24 x 64 GB (1.5 TB) SK hynix DDR5-6000 ECC RDIMM AMD EPYC 9965, EPYC 9755 Understanding the CPU's role in agentic AIDepending on where you’re at in the fast-moving world of agentic AI, you probably have a different definition of what exactly an agentic CPU is. Given the rise in prominence of agentic CPUs, the understanding of what makes a CPU tick for this type of workload has been largely defined by two companies: AMD and Nvidia. Although the points they’ve driven about concurrency and the varied work of agents are correct, it’s useful to derive a definition from how we’re seeing agentic platforms deployed right now. What to read next Modal taps Nvidia Vera CPUs after firm's internal tests show 2x throughput over Intel and AMD chips OpenAI’s Jalapeño ASICs are deployed alongside AMD EPYC ‘Turin’ CPUs as hosts, not Nvidia's Vera Arm says its AGI CPU delivers nearly 2X the performance per rack of AMD EPYC 9755 in new agentic AI CPU tests Let’s back up from there and look at real agentic workflows in action to better understand where CPUs fit into this chain. As we’ve seen with Meta Muse and OpenAI Dots, there’s a class of persistent agent that gives you a slice of compute in the cloud. These CPU-only racks communicate with inference servers to actually run the models, but their workload is defined by concurrency. It’s not about the performance of an individual sandbox but instead how each sandbox performs when the chip is fully loaded.Concurrency provides important context to some of the workloads companies like Nvidia and AMD have described. Some tool calls are more demanding, like code compilation and large database queries, but reading/writing files, running code tests, and going online in a headless browser is not demanding CPU work in isolation. When the chip is handling potentially thousands of these tool calls, however, slight advantages start to pile up. And, the CPU topology plays a bigger role in how performance is sustained as agent sessions increase.That’s one major tenet of an agentic CPU, one that can maintain performance with high concurrency. The other is variability, which touches on the CPU, but also the larger infrastructure available. Mark Lohmeyer, VP/GM of AI and computing infrastructure at Google Cloud, described an example to Tom’s Hardware about planning a vacation with an agent. Using AI to plan a vacation is just about as trite as examples get, but Lohmeyer sheds some light on the unique challenge of agentic workloads from the hyperscaler perspective.In the example, Lohmeyer described planning a vacation over the course of a month, where he would suddenly prompt the agent to do a bunch of work, but may not return to prompt again for another week. “The actual use of the underlying compute, it's happening in basically bursts, right? There's like a burst of use at the start, maybe for an hour, and then it goes away, and then a couple days later, [it] bursts again for some other purpose and goes away,” Lohmeyer said. “They're very long-running workloads, effectively long-running, but often idle, basically.”Agentic calls for a lot of power on demand, as the right alignment of this bursty work on a server with hardware contention can bring everyone’s sessions to a crawl. This factors into the type of work the CPU is doing, as well, which can include heavy code compilation, graph traversal, and large database queries. Scale that up across several agents, all with their own independent loops that don’t neatly align with each other, and the CPU problem for agentic AI becomes clear. (Image credit: The University of Texas at Austin)In the August 2026 study, Architectural Implications of Agentic AI Workflows, from researchers at The University of Texas at Austin and Microsoft Azure, the paper describes three tasks of the CPU in an agentic flow. In addition to a scheduler for GPU inference, which is how CPUs function in one-shot-style LLM queries, CPUs also serve as orchestrators for maintaining agent states and communication, and as runners that call tools and execute agent logic (often in Python). (Image credit: The University of Texas at Austin)The paper also shows this contention that can happen when multiple agents are running at once, passing requests to the GPU, receiving responses, acting, and then passing requests back. We’re looking at a cross-section of four agents over less than half a minute, and you can already see how small CPU-based tasks can align, as well as create hangs between GPU time.Nvidia has been clear that Vera is an agentic CPU, though defining the performance of an agentic loop is still a work in progress. “The industry built a pretty good way to benchmark traditional workloads,” Lohmeyer said. “I think this is happening now for GPUs and TPUs for inference, for example. I think we're going to need the same type of industry-level benchmarks for agentic workloads that are probably still emerging.”Standardized benchmarks that look at the full agentic loop aren’t available yet. We have our own internal tests that we’re running and hope to have data for soon, and we’ve seen some vendor-level benchmarking from companies like Modal, but the broader industry hasn’t come forth with a set of benchmarks for the end-to-end agentic loop along the lines of a SPEC or TPC yet.Although those tests aren’t available yet, we can still look at CPU performance through the lens of an agentic workflow, prioritizing aspects of performance that are important for agentic loops. We can also look at common workflows for agents, including code compilation for coding agents and database performance for retrieval agents. We can look at things like JSON parsing through the simdjson library, evaluating how these CPUs parse the large JSON files agents use to communicate. And we can look at the foundation of much of the AI ecosystem with Python performance.That’s the focus of our benchmarking here, to establish where Vera stands among the x86 competition from AMD and Intel in well-known benchmarks. Hopefully we’ll have the opportunity for further testing in the near future to evaluate full agentic loops once that testing procedure is finalized.Although we’re evaluating performance through an agentic lens here, Nvidia did not limit what tests we could run nor place any stipulations on our coverage. We’re thankful to Nvidia for providing us with remote access to a dual-socket Vera system for the purposes of testing, but beyond configuration checks to ensure the platform was operating as expected, we were left to run the tests we wanted to run. That includes several tests that are applicable to agentic workflows, but also tests from our general server CPU benchmarking suite, including Java, cryptography, compression, and rendering performance.A gentle reminder for readersServers are not client PCs. You have much smarter operators with deeper access to the hardware, and often a software stack that’s unique to the specific workload at minimum, and highly tweaked and optimized for that workload at a maximum. With client CPUs, we can say that an AMD X3D chip is the best for gaming, or that Intel’s latest flagship offers the highest single-threaded performance. Servers depend much more on use cases.In a typical review, we’d say that X is better than Y for Z purpose, and back that up with data. Here, that commentary is more muted. The reality is that hyperscalers maintain large fleets with a variety of hardware that can fit any purpose, and enterprises need to choose the hardware best suited not only for their operations, but also for TCO and a list of at least a dozen other variables that are specific to that business.Nvidia Vera SPEC CPU 2026 estimatesSo far, the primary benchmark we’ve had for Vera is SPEC CPU 2026 intrate, so we ran the full SPEC CPU 2026 suite to check Nvidia’s performance claims, as well as look at floating point performance. For anyone who hasn’t read SPEC CPU benchmarks before, there are a few disclaimers before heading into the results.All of the runs here are estimates, and that’s due to how SPEC reporting works. There are strict reporting rules, and we’re not reporting these results to SPEC directly. The charts say “estimated,” but the numbers aren’t a guess. We ran SPEC CPU 2026 following the standard testing procedure, using the same compiler and flags for each CPU.For the compiler, we used GCC 15.2 with a few common flags, including link-time optimization and march/mcpu to expose the correct instruction support to the compiler. We also used the general-purpose jemalloc memory allocator across all of the tests we ran. (Image credit: Tom's Hardware)Starting with the overall intrate, this is a series of applications primarily dealing with integer operations instead of floats, and the SOP is to run a copy of the application on each thread available. The test looks at what a CPU is capable of with many applications running at once, measuring throughput.Nvidia’s numbers aren’t dissimilar from our own. In the company’s white paper, it showed Vera ahead of the EPYC 9755 by 3%, and with our tests, Vera is ahead by 1.5%. Keep in mind the considerably higher 512-thread count of the 9755 system here against the 352-thread Vera system. Vera absolutely runs away with performance when breaking down the score per-core.Despite the core density of Intel’s 512-thread Xeon 6980P in a two-socket configuration, it’s not in the conversation here. Retesting with oneAPI represented an impressive 10% increase in performance with Intel-optimized binaries, but even against optimized code, Vera is 8.6% ahead with generic GCC. history.titleZh: 对Nvidia数据中心Vera CPU进行基准测试——独立Vera与Granite Rapids-AP及EPYC Turin对比测试
history.descriptionZh:
英伟达正式发布其首款深度自研的数据中心CPU——Vera，标志着该公司在AI基础设施布局上迈出关键一步。这款芯片的推出恰逢智能体AI（Agentic AI）工作流快速兴起，数据中心对CPU的需求出现前所未有的增长。尽管“专为六个月前才出现的新需求而设计”这一说法略显牵强，但Tom‘s Hardware的实测表明，英伟达对Vera的性能宣传并非空话。

**背景：智能体AI对CPU提出全新要求**

当前智能体AI的部署形态揭示了CPU在其中的关键角色。以Meta Muse和OpenAI Dots为代表的一类持久化智能体，为用户提供云端计算切片，这些纯CPU机架与推理服务器通信来运行模型，其负载的核心特征是并发性——关键不在于单个沙箱的性能，而在于芯片满载时每个沙箱的表现。部分工具调用（如代码编译、大型数据库查询）计算密集，而文件读写、代码测试、无头浏览器访问等单独看并不繁重，但当芯片同时处理数千个此类调用时，细微优势就会累积放大，CPU拓扑结构对高并发下性能的持续性影响显著。

另一大特征是负载的突发性。Google Cloud AI与计算基础设施副总裁兼总经理Mark Lohmeyer以规划度假为例说明：用户可能在月初突然让智能体执行大量工作，随后一周不再使用，计算资源呈爆发式使用后长期空闲。这种长时运行但经常闲置的负载模式，要求CPU能够应对多个独立循环、彼此不对齐的智能体同时运行带来的资源争抢。2026年8月，德克萨斯大学奥斯汀分校与微软Azure研究人员发表的《智能体AI工作流的架构影响》论文指出，CPU在智能体流程中承担三类任务：作为GPU推理的调度器、作为维护智能体状态与通信的编排器、以及作为调用工具和执行智能体逻辑（通常用Python）的执行器。

**技术架构：Olympus核心与SCF互连架构**

Vera基于Armv9.2-A架构，采用英伟达首款自研核心“Olympus”，共88核176线程，通过英伟达“空间多线程”技术实现每核双线程。芯片采用10宽解码设计，并搭载第二代可扩展一致性架构（SCF）。SCF是一个在芯片裸片上分布L3缓存的网状结构，片内带宽可达3.4 TB/s，对Vera的整体性能至关重要。相比采用现成Arm核心设计的Grace，Vera在几乎所有方面都有显著提升。

规格方面，Vera每核配备2 MB L2缓存，每CPU配备164 MB L3缓存；支持最高1.5 TB的SOCAMM2 LPDDR5X内存，速率达9600 MT/s；聚合内存带宽最高1.2 TB/s，每核约14 GB/s，超过AMD密集型Turin设计的两倍；芯片间通过高速C2C互连，双路间带宽可达1.8 TB/s。I/O方面提供88条PCIe 6.4通道（纯CPU配置）或96条（Vera Rubin配置），支持x2拆分和CXL 3.1；可配置TDP为250W至450W。

**测试平台与性能表现**

测试对比平台包括：双路英伟达MGX Vera参考平台（1.5 TB三星LPDDR5-9600 ECC SOCAMM2）、双路Supermicro SYS-222HA搭载英特尔至强6980P（1.5 TB美光DDR5-8800 ECC MRDIMM）、以及双路AMD Volcano参考平台搭载EPYC 9965和EPYC 9755（1.5 TB SK海力士DDR5-6000 ECC RDIMM）。需注意服务器评测与消费级PC不同，超大规模厂商维护着适配各种用途的多样化硬件集群，企业选型还需综合考虑总体拥有成本等十余项变量。

SPEC CPU 2026整数吞吐率测试中，Vera领先EPYC 9755约1.5%（英伟达白皮书称领先3%），但9755系统拥有512线程，而Vera系统为352线程；按每核性能计算，Vera大幅领先。面对英特尔512线程的双路至强6980P，即便使用oneAPI优化二进制带来约10%的性能提升，Vera使用通用GCC编译仍领先8.6%。浮点测试中Vera同样登顶，PALM测试展现了第二代SCF的优势，ROMS、Marian和LBM则体现了内存带宽的强势，仅在FemFlow和CACTUS等少数项目落后。

Python性能是当前最接近智能体AI直接基准的指标——LangGraph、CrewAI、AutoGen等主流智能体框架均以Python为基础。PyBench测试中Vera领先EPYC 9755约4%，在PyPerformance的绝大多数细分项目（解释器启动、正则表达式、完整应用）中全面领先，仅在少数Web服务器相关测试中落后。Llama.cpp纯CPU推理测试中，单路至强6980P在提示处理环节领先，这很可能得益于英特尔的AI专用指令集扩展，预计AMD将在Zen 6中扩展此类指令支持以拉平差距。

内存带宽方面，STREAM基准验证了英伟达的宣传：Vera内存总线宽度超过Grace两倍以上，配合LPDDR5X-9600，在英伟达建议的OpenMP“spread”策略下（将进程尽可能分散以减少缓存/内存争用），Vera获得大幅带宽提升，而AMD和英特尔平台在该设置下略有回退。MBW测试同样表现强劲。不过CacheBench的读写修改组合测试中Vera垫底，缓存性能略逊于竞品，但被内存带宽优势所掩盖。

压缩负载呈现分化：Zstd默认3级和最高19级压缩（标准与长模式）中Vera均登顶，但解压环节Turin反超，Vera与双路6980P相当或略低；7-Zip测试中两款Turin配置领先，Vera在压缩和解压两项均落后于双路6980P。

Java测试中，SciMark综合分由基于Zen 5的9755领先，但Vera在FFT、稀疏矩阵乘法、蒙特卡洛模拟等纯科学运算中保持强势，在密集LU矩阵分解和Jacobi SOR中落后。数据库表现亮眼：SQLite最大线程测试中Vera仅输给单路6980P，在64线程和128线程同口径测试中领先；ClickHouse冷缓存首轮运行中Vera比双路EPYC 9755快近40%，第二、三轮则与对手持平。JSON解析（simdjson）因依赖现代SIMD指令，Turin凭借原生AVX-512执行自然领先。加密负载是明显短板，John The Ripper密码破解大幅落后，OpenSSL也不敌竞品的庞大核心阵列。

HPC测试中Vera在FFTE离散傅里叶变换、Octave和CloverLeaf中登顶，但在m-queens等密集数学运算中居中游，在高度线程化的Primesieve中因核心数劣势落后。代码编译对编码类智能体意义重大，Vera在GCC定时编译中领先双路9755达12%，但在LLVM编译（Makefile和Ninja两种方式）中垫底，ImageMagick和PHP编译表现强劲，Godot编译略逊于双路9755。编码与渲染并非Vera主攻方向，AV1编码中9755领先，x265编码Vera胜出但优势小于AV1项目中9755的25%以上领先幅度；C-Ray和POV-Ray测试中Vera甚至超越768线程的双路EPYC 9965，OSPRay实时路径追踪登顶，但科学可视化项目落后，dim_512子项中AMD凭借强大的AVX-512性能达到Vera的三到四倍。

**市场定位与影响**

Vera并非英伟达首款数据中心CPU，却是公司首次以对待加速器同等的力度大力推进的产品。其独特能力与拓扑结构在适配的工作负载中往往能越级发挥。但这是一款88核单一配置的芯片，面对的是以细粒度SKU列表覆盖广泛特定工作负载的成熟市场。英伟达Ian Buck在3月发布时即表示：“世界不会由单一SKU的CPU来服务，这也不是我们的意图。”尽管如此，Vera相对当代x86处理器的性能表现证明，英伟达进军独立数据中心CPU并非玩票，其意义远超超大规模厂商此前推出的各类“积木式”Arm芯片，至少足以让AMD和英特尔认真对待。x86阵营的反击即将到来：Zen 6预计年内铺开，英特尔Diamond Rapids瞄准2027年发布。

history.content: Maine Sen. Susan Collins, a Republican, was midway through defending her record during the final debate of the midterms when an audience member cut her short.“I’m terrified,” a man shouted. “AI data centers are destroying our climate. They are poisoning our water.” Collins brushed off the outburst, tying the man to her Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson. But the fear echoing through the auditorium wasn’t so easily dismissed. Just days before voters head to the polls, the rapid expansion of resource-hungry data centers has exploded into one of Maine’s most volatile campaign issues.Maine drew national headlines in April when the state Legislature passed what would have been the nation’s first statewide moratorium on large data centers — had Gov. Janet Mills not vetoed the bill 10 days later. But the fight hasn’t slowed down, with towns across the state adopting temporary moratoriums or putting the question of data center expansion to voters this November. In a September poll of Mainers by UMass Lowell and YouGov, 76 percent of respondents said they oppose building a data center in their community, with 58 percent strongly opposed.Maine’s hotly contested Senate race is set to be the most expensive Senate race per capita that the US has ever seen, with Democrats spending a projected $81 million and Republicans $114 million. Much of that campaign cash has come from the very industry Mainers and rural voters across the country have been fighting for more than a year. The outcome of the race will help determine which party controls the Senate and help shape federal data center and AI policy, impacting data center construction not just for Maine residents, but for the entire country.Cheap land, rich waterMaine and other rural states are becoming prime targets for new data centers. While cities run short on land and power, Maine has abundant cheap land, vacant industrial mills and buildings, and ample access to water, thanks to its numerous rivers and waterways. Recognizing the high stakes, major tech companies and private equity firms tied to data centers and AI have invested millions in the midterms to win over skeptical locals.The issue has sparked fierce local debate, leading towns and cities across the state to enact temporary bans this summer.Molly White, the researcher, writer, and software engineer behind Tech Influence Watch, says that voters are paying a lot of attention to the issue because they connect data centers to rising costs for utilities. As White points out, many Mainers are also already feeling the pinch due to record-high heating oil costs this fall, and “they’re now looking at an election where the question is, is this candidate going to invite a data center to move in next door, and then my electricity prices go up, or the knock-on effects are going to hurt me even more when I’m already in very dire straits?” she said.White launched her site in 2024 to track crypto spending in political races, but has since expanded it to monitor AI and Big Tech investments. White says the playbook that AI and data center backers are using in the midterms is very similar to the one the cryptocurrency industry used in 2024.“There’s a lot going on in this election,” White says, “but I do think it has been a big issue in Maine and across the country, where you’ll go to a political event, you’ll see people asking questions of candidates, and AI keeps coming up. Certainly there’s a lot of questions about the economy, the war, all these different things, but AI is the new one.”“Certainly there’s a lot of questions about the economy, the war, all these different things, but AI is the new one.”— Molly WhiteData center developers and their political allies often sell rural Maine communities on long-term job creation — a promise economists say rarely materializes. In reality, economic research indicates that most data centers create virtually no net employment once construction is complete.Historically, Maine’s industry has centered around lumber and timber, shipbuilding, commercial fishing, textiles, and pulp and paper manufacturing. The timber industry contributed around $8.3 billion to Maine’s economy in 2024, but Donald Trump’s tariffs and rising operating costs have hit it hard, resulting in mill closures and layoffs.Mark Brewer, who chairs the political science department at the University of Maine, says Maine’s history complicates the debate. These former mill towns jump at the chance to rebuild their local tax bases and infrastructure, but past boom-and-bust cycles make residents cautious.“Maine has a long history of extractive industries providing jobs,” Brewer says, which allowed Mainers to tolerate these industries despite the state’s environmental focus. With data centers thus far, he says, “the jobs part of it’s not there. It’s one thing to put up with a paper mill that’s employing three shifts of 1,000 workers, right? Data centers aren’t doing that.”For many rural Mainers, the question is not only whether a data center will bring jobs back, but whether to trust the companies promising them or the government helping make the deal, said Nicholas Jacobs, the director of the Public Policy Lab at Colby College in Maine. These residents say they’re concerned about the opaque ownership of these data centers, limited long-term employment, and the risk of wealth being extracted from rural communities.Tech millions fuel Collins’ reelection war chestTech and AI interests see an ally in Susan Collins, the 73-year-old Republican chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. Like most congressional Republicans, she has largely supported data centers and AI, though she has said she believes data centers should be evaluated on an individual basis. Collins has even used her position as head of the Appropriations Committee to secure $6.2 million in federal funding for a high-performance computing hub data center in central Maine, which is designed to bolster localized AI and biotech research. Her stance has brought in a tremendous amount of campaign donations from Big Tech, AI, and data center donors for her reelection bid.Collins’ individual donors include Alex Karp, the cofounder and CEO of Palantir; Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz of VC firm Andreessen Horowitz, which heavily backs data centers; and others from Google, Meta, and Microsoft. According to White’s donation tracker, Collins has received $325,644 from AI and crypto donors. Nearly 100 billionaires have donated to Collins’ reelection bid in some form or another.“It’s one thing to put up with a paper mill that’s employing three shifts of 1,000 workers, right? Data centers aren’t doing that.”— Mark BrewerSuper PACs like the Republican Senate Leadership Fund dumped nearly $42 million into ads across Maine. Elon Musk gave $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund this summer, and has spent around $450 million of his own money to support Republicans in the midterms. Musk’s America PAC has spent around $2.1 million in Maine. Pine Tree Results PAC, to which Collins and her husband have personal ties, put $29.1 million into the race to support her. Stephen Schwarzman from Blackstone has donated $2 million this year to Pine Tree Results.A recent FEC report flagged by the Maine Newsroom shows that Musk’s corporate SpaceX PAC gave $55,000 to Collins’ Victory Committee in August and another $50,000 to the Pine Tree Results PAC.The campaign and PAC money appears to flow in support of just one candidate, too. Collins’ opponent Troy Jackson only recently filed his FEC paperwork, which shows no obvious data center, AI, or Big Tech ties, though it does show at least four billionaire donors. However, Jackson’s stance is similar to Collins’, and he focuses largely on putting guardrails in place for AI and data center development. He has said he wants to ensure union jobs for the buildout and maintenance of data centers in the state.Collins’ ties to data centers don’t stop with her donors. Her family has actual stakes in the AI boom. Earlier this month, Forbes ranked Collins’ household fifth in the Senate for AI- and data center-linked investments, with an estimated $300,000 to $800,000 held in her husband Thomas Daffron’s name.Daffron is a former lobbyist and was paid consulting fees in 2025 by the lobbying firm of Scott Reed. Reed chairs Pine Tree Results, the super PAC with close ties to Collins. And according to American Journal News and The New York Times, Reed’s firm lobbied for a developer that has built data centers in Maine. Collins’ financial disclosure shows that she and her husband hold assets worth anywhere from $4 million to $10 million.Jackson, who started as a logger before he was elected to the state Senate, has most recently earned money from consulting, and he and his wife hold assets worth anywhere from $147,000 to $430,000. He doesn’t have any reported financial ties to data centers, AI, or Big Tech interests.Outside money and extractive boom-and-bust fears fuel backlashBillionaire influence tends to spark partisan backlash, White notes, adding that Mainers resent wealthy outsiders trying to buy their votes. Jacobs agrees, noting that many Maine voters harbor a deep, long-standing skepticism toward anyone from “away” looking to exploit local resources.“Rural wealth exists, but it is extracted out of the community, and that’s the game of rural living,” Jacobs says. “You harvest your timber; you send it away. You harvest your crops; you send them away. It’s extractive, but there’s a fine line between an extractive economy and an exploitive economy. And so I do think that there is a history and maybe even a culture of wariness towards that form of exploitation.”Brewer says he is skeptical that the huge amount of campaign spending will sway rural voters’ views about data centers. If anything, voters may punish Collins for her ties to Elon Musk and other unpopular tech billionaires.“Rural wealth exists, but it is extracted out of the community, and that’s the game of rural living.”— Nicholas JacobsMuch of the campaign spending from the super PACS with a vested interest in data centers and AI has flooded the airwaves and mailboxes with hostile attack ads, Jacobs and Brewer note. With broadcast television inventory completely sold out, campaigns have shifted money into radio, social media, and direct mail. The sheer volume has pushed voters past their breaking point, Brewer says, calling the contest “the most negative race” he has tracked in 25 years of observing Maine politics.According to a recent Maine Monitor report, as of mid-October, $54 million has been spent or committed for negative attack ads, and nearly all of it is coming from outside PACs financed by Big Tech and data center supporters, not the candidates’ campaigns. While no ads have focused specifically on Collins’ support for data centers and AI, some have targeted her ties to Big Tech, billionaires, and data centers through her husband. The National Republican Senatorial Committee tried to tie Troy Jackson to Senate Democrats’ opposition to the Husted legislation in September in a press release.“That is where the overwhelming amount of money is going,” Jacobs says about the attack ads. “It’s ads, and then paying consultants to write the ads, polling, paying the consultants to do the polls, right? The worst case is that it tarnishes the image of democracy in voters’ minds, and I think that is the most significant consequence beyond any quid pro quo relationship.”As Jacobs notes, many Maine voters, especially independents, are conflicted about data center investment in the state. They are deeply attached to their community and wary of outsiders changing it, while also worried their children won’t be able to afford to stay or find good jobs without the influx of tech money.“I think many people throughout Maine worry about the future and whether or not their children will be able to afford to live there,” he says. “Whether there will be jobs. Both of these things are true … Data centers just seem to be this symbolic flashpoint of that tension in rural living.”

history.titleZh: 缅因州的数据中心反抗将决定谁掌控参议院
history.descriptionZh:
距离美国中期选举仅数天，缅因州参议院选战已因AI数据中心快速扩张而演变为全州最敏感的议题之一。背景是：缅因州议会今年4月通过一项旨在暂停大型数据中心建设的法案，若生效将成为全美首个州级大型数据中心暂停令，但州长珍妮特·米尔斯在10天后否决。此后，全州多个城镇自行通过临时禁令，或把数据中心扩张问题交由11月选民公投。UMass Lowell与YouGov9月民调显示，76%的缅因州受访者反对在所在社区建设数据中心，58%强烈反对。文章中的辩论现场，一名观众高喊“我很害怕”，称AI数据中心正在破坏气候、毒害水源，反映出当地对资源消耗、电价上涨和环境风险的焦虑。

从产业逻辑看，AI数据中心是支撑大模型训练和推理的算力基础设施，需要大规模服务器和GPU集群、持续稳定的电力供应以及大量冷却用水。报道并未讨论具体芯片架构、能效技术或冷却创新，因此其“创新点”主要体现在产业选址和政治动员层面：数据中心开发商正把目光转向土地和电力成本较低、水源充足的农村地区。缅因州因廉价土地、空置工业厂房和众多河流水源成为目标。开发商常承诺长期就业，但经济研究显示，数据中心在建设完成后创造的净就业岗位极少。缅因州政治学教授马克·布鲁尔举例说，造纸厂可雇佣三班共1000名工人，而数据中心做不到这一点。该州木材业2024年贡献约83亿美元，但受关税和运营成本上升冲击，工厂关闭和裁员使前工业城镇既渴望重建税基，又担心重演资源开采型经济的繁荣—萧条循环。科尔比学院尼古拉斯·雅各布斯指出，缅因州有“资源被开采后运走”的历史，居民对外来资本提取本地财富保持警惕。

竞选资金使争议进一步升温。缅因州这场选战预计将成为美国人均花费最高的参议院选举：民主党预计支出8100万美元，共和党1.14亿美元。共和党候选人、73岁的参议院拨款委员会主席苏珊·柯林斯大体支持数据中心和AI，但表示应逐案评估；她利用拨款委员会职位为缅因州中部一个高性能计算中心数据中心争取620万美元联邦资金，用于促进本地AI和生物技术研究。追踪政治支出的Molly White称，柯林斯已从AI和加密相关捐赠者获得325,644美元，个人捐赠者包括Palantir联合创始人兼CEO亚历克斯·卡普、风投a16z的马克·安德森和本·霍洛维茨，以及谷歌、Meta和微软相关人士；近100名亿万富翁以不同形式向她捐款。福布斯本月将柯林斯家庭列为参议院AI和数据中心相关投资第五名，估计其丈夫托马斯·达夫龙名下持有30万至80万美元相关资产；达夫龙曾是游说人士，2025年从与柯林斯关系密切的超级PAC“Pine Tree Results”主席斯科特·里德的游说公司获得咨询费。柯林斯夫妇披露资产在400万至1000万美元之间。其对手特洛伊·杰克逊曾是伐木工，后来从事咨询，夫妇资产在14.7万至43万美元之间，没有明显的数据中心、AI或大型科技财务关系；他的立场与柯林斯相近，也强调对AI和数据中心开发设限，并希望确保建设和维护中的工会就业。

外部资金规模同样惊人。与共和党参议院领导基金相关的超级PAC在缅因州投放近4200万美元广告；埃隆·马斯克今夏向该基金捐赠1.58亿美元，并已自掏约4.5亿美元支持共和党中期选举，其America PAC在缅因州支出约210万美元；“Pine Tree Results”投入2910万美元支持柯林斯，黑石的斯蒂芬·施瓦茨曼今年向其捐赠200万美元；马斯克旗下SpaceX PAC还向柯林斯胜利委员会捐赠5.5万美元、向Pine Tree Results捐赠5万美元。截至10月中旬，负面攻击广告已支出或承诺5400万美元，几乎全部来自大型科技和数据中心支持者资助的外部PAC。广告虽未直接集中攻击柯林斯支持数据中心，但试图把她与大型科技、亿万富翁和数据中心利益联系起来。布鲁尔称这是他观察缅因州政治25年来“最负面”的选战；雅各布斯则担心，巨额外部资金和攻击广告会损害选民对民主的信心。

这场选举的结果不仅决定参议院控制权，也将影响联邦数据中心和AI政策，进而影响全美数据中心建设。对缅因州农村选民而言，核心矛盾是：既要争取税基、基础设施和子女留在当地的就业机会，又担心电价上涨、水资源和气候成本、就业承诺落空以及外来资本提取本地财富。Molly White指出，AI和数据中心金主在中期选举中的策略与加密行业2024年的政治投放非常相似。AI正成为继经济、战争等传统议题之后的新选举议题，而缅因州则成为AI数据中心扩张与农村社区利益冲突的集中缩影。

history.description: A criminal investigation into the environmental damage caused by Google’s Finnish subsidiary has been launched.

Tuike Finland Oy is being investigated after five complaints were received regarding the Muhos data center project, according to an official police statement published today [machine translation].Go deeper with TH Premium: AI and data centers (Image credit: Microsoft)The data center cooling state of playThe custom AI ASIC state of play America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the priceGTC 2026: Ian Buck press Q&A transcript — VP of Hyperscale and HPC speaks out on shelving CPX and shipping LPU decode this yearDemand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsibleThe police say that the investigation is backed by Finland’s Licensing and Supervision Authority (LVV). Google/Tuike Finland Oy is accused of suspected breaches of environmental law and environmental damage. Other lesser criminal offenses related to ambiguities and shortcomings in the drainage and water management are also being investigated.Since Google representatives have previously publicly apologized for the unauthorized forest clearings near Muhos, which have turned 816 acres of forest into an expanse of mud, there seems little doubt it is guilty of some wrongdoing. Rather, it is the scale of the punishment and any proposed remedies that will probably be of most concern to execs from the tech giant now.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: As well as the awful mess Google has made near Muhos, it seems to have also jumped the gun and plowed ahead with data center development by clearing 500 acres of forest near Otanmäki.Though the horse has already bolted, Reuters reports that a Google rep said the company would cooperate with the ⁠police investigation and continue to focus on maintaining compliance at its sites. history.titleZh: 谷歌因未经批准建设AI数据中心致森林砍伐而面临刑事调查
history.descriptionZh:
芬兰警方已对谷歌芬兰子公司 Tuike Finland Oy 展开刑事调查，焦点是该公司的 Muhos 数据中心项目涉嫌造成环境损害。警方称，调查源于针对该项目收到的五起投诉，并得到芬兰许可与监管局（LVV）支持。谷歌/Tuike Finland Oy 被指涉嫌违反环境法并造成环境损害；警方还在调查与排水和水管理中的模糊之处、缺陷相关的较轻刑事违法行为。此前谷歌代表已就 Muhos 附近未经授权清理森林公开道歉，相关清理使 816 英亩森林变成泥地。报道还称，谷歌在 Otanmäki 附近清除了 500 英亩森林，被认为在数据中心开发上“抢跑”。路透社称，谷歌代表表示将配合警方调查，并继续关注其场址的合规性。

这起事件并非芯片或数据中心冷却技术的产品发布，原文没有披露具体 AI 芯片、服务器架构、冷却方案或性能参数，因此无法从报道中分析“核心技术原理和创新点”。可确认的背景是：AI 数据中心需要大量土地、电力和冷却资源，谷歌将芬兰视为有吸引力的选址，原因包括气候凉爽、电力成本较低、政府对 AI 项目的支持、人口密度低以及当地抗议倾向相对较低。但数据中心建设也带来森林清理、排水和水管理、施工与运营噪声、污染、公用事业资源竞争等环境与社区问题。报道提到，当地居民对数据中心开发的担忧还包括电价可能上涨 40%；此前甚至出现狼因栖息地破坏而进入芬兰村庄的报道。就可比数据而言，原文主要给出的是环境与合规层面的数字：Muhos 项目收到五起投诉，Muhos 附近 816 英亩森林被清理，Otanmäki 附近另有 500 英亩森林被清理，以及可能 40% 的电价上涨影响；并没有提供算力、能效、PUE、芯片型号等性能对比数据。

从技术影响和应用场景看，这一案件反映的是 AI 基础设施快速扩张与当地环境监管、水资源管理、生态保护和社区接受度之间的冲突。对谷歌而言，芬兰的凉爽气候和廉价电力有利于降低数据中心冷却与运营成本，但森林清理和排水问题可能带来刑事调查、整改要求、项目延期和声誉风险。对行业而言，数据中心选址将越来越需要把环境影响评估、排水与水管理、生物多样性保护和社区沟通纳入前期规划；否则，AI 算力基础设施建设可能因合规和公众反对而受阻。芬兰政府代表尚未就此案发表评论。总体看，报道的核心不是技术突破，而是谷歌在芬兰的数据中心项目因涉嫌环境违法而面临刑事调查，以及 AI 数据中心扩张带来的环境合规和社区关系挑战。

history.title: Intel confirms Nova Lake CPUs will use advanced 18A-P node, more details at CES
history.description: Intel's next-gen Nova Lake desktop processors will be the first client product to use Intel's enhanced 18A-P node, CEO Lip-Bu Tan confirmed in the company's Q3 2026 earnings call.
history.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 2 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Intel's next-gen Nova Lake desktop processors will be the first client product to use Intel's enhanced 18A-P node, CEO Lip-Bu Tan confirmed in the company's Q3 2026 earnings call. The chief executive also said that the company intends to share more about Nova Lake at CES in January. The company's chief financial officer shared that Intel intends to take Panther Lake capacity offline to build more Granite Rapids data center CPUs.Go deeper with TH Premium: CPU (Image credit: Tom's Hardware)Intel VP Robert Hallock sets Nova Lake expectations, teases return to Raptor Lake for DDR4 platformsCPU scaling with DLSSIntel's one-two punch plan in desktop CPUs is taking shapeBenchmarking AMD's BC-250, offering Steam Machine-like performance at half the priceAMD splits Zen 7 into three EPYC families for 2028 and starts selling server CPUs by the agent "Nova Lake, our first Intel 18A-P client product, is tracking ahead of schedule, with design wins expecting to be twice those of Panther Lake at launch," Tan said in his prepared remarks. "We look forward to sharing more at CES in January."There has been a lot of speculation about what node Intel's Nova Lake CPUs will use, with the rumor mill ping-ponging between Intel 18A and TSMC's N2P. Current speculation says the chip will use 18A-P for the SoC tile while using TSMC's N2P for the compute tile. It seems unlikely that Intel would use its most advanced node for an SoC tile, though it's possible.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: Regardless, Nova Lake chips will use 18A-P in some regard. Intel announced in June that 18A-P had entered risk production, and at Hot Chips in August, Intel revealed its next-gen Xeon 7 Diamond Rapids will be the company's first server products to use the enhanced node.Compared to 18A, which is available in Panther Lake and Wildcat Lake products currently, 18A-P comes with a 9% improvement in speed at iso-power, or an 18% reduction in power at iso-speed. Intel has described 18A-P as a drop-in replacement for 18A, allowing designs built for 18A to instead leverage 18A-P without any extra engineering work. You may like Details about Intel's next-gen Nova Lake CPUs keep leaking Intel's Core Ultra 400 'Nova Lake' launch schedule leaks out Leaked Intel Nova Lake product list has three 'BFC' chips with up to 144MB of game-boosting L3 cache For 18A products, Intel says its new Wildcat Lake products that have shown up in devices like the Framework Laptop 12 are increasingly popular. "Demand for our Wildcat Lake is outstripping supply," said Tan. Intel says that 18A products now make up a third of client CPU revenue, up from less than 5% in Q1.It makes sense that those products would be popular given the current environment. Tan said that Intel's OEM partners are "aggressively managing inventory to match softer sell-through," which means buying less to match the demand in the market. Intel's David Zinsner said the company expects the company's client business to decline by "more than 20%" in the next quarter."Stay On the Cutting Edge: Get the Tom's Hardware NewsletterGet Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsorsZinsner warned of a further contraction in the PC market, describing a sustained decline in the size of the market over the next year, at least. "We expect the 2026 PC unit [Total Addressable Market] to decline approximately 12%, with second half units down more than 20%. We do not expect a sustained recovery until memory availability improves and pricing begins to normalize," Zinsner said. "For 2027, we're planning a PC unit TAM to decline roughly 10%."Taking the comments together, Intel is saying that it expects the market itself to shrink significantly over the next year due to memory prices. It's not a situation of demand outstripping supply, at least not directly like the case of a component shortage. Rather, it's a pullback from direct customers, OEMs, and IT departments from spending, which is more significant.Although Intel says the client PC market is shrinking, the company says that its long-term outlook remains positive. "We think next year, and in future years, we're a market-share-gain type of environment... we do think the PC is going to through a renaissance despite [memory shortage]," said Zinsner.Despite the optimism, Zinsner said that Intel is taking some of its client capacity offline to build more data center products. In response to a question about reallocating wafers from client products, here's what the executive said: "Answer: Yes... What we're taking offline to put Intel 3 into Oregon is 18A wafers, which were generally going to build Panther Lake products, so we see the opportunity with some of that capacity freed up to go produce more data center wafers." history.titleZh: 英特尔确认Nova Lake CPU将采用先进18A-P工艺，更多细节将在CES公布
history.descriptionZh:
英特尔CEO陈立武在2026年第三季度财报电话会上确认，下一代桌面处理器Nova Lake将成为首款采用增强版Intel 18A-P节点的客户端产品，并计划在明年1月CES上披露更多细节。陈立武称，Nova Lake进度超前，发布时的设计订单预计将达到Panther Lake的两倍。此前业界对Nova Lake采用何种制程猜测不断，在Intel 18A与台积电N2P之间反复摇摆；当前传闻称其SoC tile可能使用18A-P，计算tile使用台积电N2P。将最先进节点用于SoC tile并不常见，但并非不可能；无论如何，Nova Lake都会在部分模块使用18A-P。18A-P已于6月进入风险生产，英特尔在8月Hot Chips上还表示，下一代Xeon 7 Diamond Rapids将是首款采用该增强节点的服务器产品。

在技术层面，18A-P是Intel 18A的性能增强版本。相比已用于Panther Lake和Wildcat Lake的18A，18A-P在同等功耗下速度提升9%，或在同等速度下功耗降低18%。英特尔将其描述为18A的“drop-in replacement”，即针对18A设计的产品无需额外工程工作即可迁移到18A-P，这有助于降低客户采用新节点的成本和产品迭代风险。Wildcat Lake已在Framework Laptop 12等设备中出现，陈立武称其需求超过供应；18A产品目前已占英特尔客户端CPU营收的三分之一，而第一季度还不足5%，显示18A家族的量产爬坡和客户接受度明显改善，也为Nova Lake采用18A-P奠定基础。

市场与产能方面，英特尔CFO David Zinsner表示，公司计划将部分Panther Lake产能下线，以生产更多Granite Rapids数据中心CPU。原本用于Panther Lake的18A晶圆产能将被释放，在俄勒冈转向Intel 3，并增加数据中心晶圆产出。英特尔预计客户端业务下季度将下降超过20%。PC市场方面，Zinsner预计2026年PC单位总可寻址市场（TAM）将下降约12%，下半年降幅超过20%；在内存供应改善和价格正常化之前，不会出现持续复苏；2027年PC单位TAM预计再下降约10%。他强调，这并不是组件短缺导致需求超过供给，而是直接客户、OEM和IT部门支出回撤；OEM合作伙伴也在积极管理库存，以匹配较软的终端销售。尽管短期收缩，英特尔仍坚持长期乐观判断，认为未来将处于市场份额增长环境，并认为PC将迎来复兴，即便存在内存短缺。

整体来看，Nova Lake若按计划在CES亮相并采用18A-P，将成为英特尔展示先进制程在客户端落地、吸引OEM设计的关键产品；设计订单翻倍有助于扩大平台覆盖。18A-P的等功耗性能提升和低迁移成本，可改善台式机能效与性能竞争力，并与台积电N2P在部分tile上形成混合制程方案。同时，英特尔将部分客户端产能转向数据中心产品，反映其在PC下行周期优先保障高价值服务器业务的策略，可能影响客户端供应节奏。英特尔正试图在制程推进、客户端产品路线和数据中心产能分配之间取得平衡：短期PC市场受内存价格压制，长期则押注份额提升和PC复苏。
